newsitem.title: USA: Progress on U.S. business problems with Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: Progress on U.S. business problems with Ukraine.

text.p: Ahead of next week's meeting between Vice President Al Gore and Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, the Ukrainian and U.S. ambassadors on Friday reported progress in combatting corruption concerns and problems related to U.S. business deals.
Ukrainian Ambassador Yuri Shcherbak said at least five cases involving American companies had been solved and others were on their way to resolution.

The cases are expected to be discussed in detail when Gore and Kuchma meet on Monday in New York to follow up discussions they had in May in Washington on Ukraine's economic reform progress and its investment climate, officials said.

The United States has put pressure on Ukraine to end corruption and speed up reform. U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Miller said the country "has not only made a verbal commitment (to meet U.S. concerns), it is following through with practical steps."

"Most of the cases have been solved and the ones that are not are in a rigorous transparent process. We're very satisfied that what is happening is the complete response to discussions between Gore and Kuchma in Washington in May."

Cases Shcherbak described as "solved" involved the U.S. firms Alliant-Kiev, which will work with a Ukrainian corporation on conventional arms dismantling; Cargill Inc. US001041053=, a Minnesota-based grain giant whose projects have been declared "priorities" in Ukraine's privatisation of agriculture, and Boeing Co., from whom Ukraine is buying two 767 jets.
Other solved cases are Kiev-Atlantic and Monsanto, for whom Ukraine approved a guarantee of $27.8 million in credit for a joint venture with the Agrodon Corp, he said.

Another case, involving Gala-Radio, is "very complicated" and being reviewed, with the involvement of two U.S. Commerce Department lawyers, he said. Claims by Hughes Network Systems, R&J Trading, Perekhid-Media and NCH Advisors are being reviewed on a "fast track system" by the government, he said.

On economic reform, he said subsidies to the coal, agro-industrial and metallurgical industries have been reduced and are being replaced by a market credit system that would force industries to compete with international markets.
Also, he said, inflation "has been virtually eliminated," and it is hoped parliament will soon adopt a new budget.
Budget approval is a key item on a list of 41 conditions Ukraine must meet to qualify for a $2.4-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan from the International Monetary Fund.
Ukraine is moving to stabilise and reduce taxes, which U.S. officials believe would foster investment and integrate the country's underground economy with its official economy.
Miller said "this is a very difficult process" but Ukraine is "going in the right direction."

Kuchma, under pressure from Western donors to fire Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, removed him by decree on Thursday. Diplomatic and business sources said Kuchma faced demands for Lazarenko's head from Western officials who saw him as an anti-reformist force.

Shcherbak said the new acting prime minister, Vasyl Durdynets, was in Washington two weeks ago as coordinator of his government's anti-corruption committee and held talks with FBI Director Louis Freeh, among others.
